V0.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Norwegian: Solheim 22; Jewish: *Neuman.
V0.p: A general heading for motifs about religious services and rites of worship.

V1.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 649b; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 214, *Boberg.
V1.p: A general heading for the kinds of beings or things that people worship.

V1.1.p: Worship of particular named gods or goddesses.

V1.1.1.p: Worship of a single god, as opposed to many gods.

V1.2.p: Worship of spirits and supernatural beings.

V1.2.1.p: Worship of fairies, the small supernatural beings of folklore.

V1.2.2.p: Worship of the devil as a supernatural being.

V1.2.3.p: Worship of a spirit or being called "disar" in Thompson's source; the headline gives only this name, so its nature is not further described here.

V1.2.4.p: Worship of angels, the heavenly messenger beings of religious belief.

V1.3.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics I 425—67; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 411 s.v. “Ahnenfiguren”; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 160; Society Islands: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 561; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/619); Africa (Cameroon): Mansfield 233, (Fang): Trilles 140.
V1.3.p: Worship of dead ancestors, honoring one's forebears as sacred.

V1.4.p: A general heading for worship of the sky, sun, moon, and other heavenly bodies.

V1.4.1.p: Worship of the sky itself as a divine being or power.

V1.4.2.r: (Cf. A220.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 12.

V1.4.4.p: Stars are worshipped as sacred or divine beings.

V1.5.p: Natural phenomena such as weather and light are treated as objects of worship.

V1.5.1.p: Clouds are worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.2.p: Thunder is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.3.p: The wind is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.4.p: A storm is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.5.p: The dawn is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.6.p: Light is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.6.1.p: The rainbow is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.5.7.p: Frost is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.p: The basic elements of nature such as earth, water and fire are treated as objects of worship.

V1.6.1.p: The earth itself is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.1.1.r: (Cf. A495.) Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 65ff., (1931) 47ff.
V1.6.1.1.p: Mountains and hills are worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.2.p: Water is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.2.1.p: Rivers and lakes are regarded as sacred and treated with reverence.

V1.6.2.2.p: The sea is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.3.r: (Cf. A493.) Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 202c; Penzer III 160; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
V1.6.3.p: Fire is worshipped as sacred or divine.

V1.6.3.1.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 202b; Penzer I 260, II 247—55; Irish myth: *Cross.
V1.6.3.1.p: A fire kept as sacred and tended in worship.

V1.6.3.1.1.p: A sacrificial fire from which all other fires must be lit, so that every household or altar fire traces back to it.

V1.6.4.p: Worship of minerals and metals: people revere certain rocks, ores or metals as holy objects.

V1.6.4.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 322, Boberg, Schmidt DF XXXIX 86ff.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 88ff.; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 382.
V1.6.4.1.p: Sacred stones: a particular stone or stones are treated as holy and worshipped.

V1.6.4.2.p: Sacred shells: a particular shell or shells are treated as holy and worshipped.

V1.7.r: (Cf. A430, C51.2.2.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 611b; *Penzer II 96 n. 1, VII 162 n. 1; Schmidt Brandtrær og Ulykkestrær Danske Studier (1928) 54ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 214; S. A. Indian (Antilles): Alexander Lat. Am. 25f.
V1.7.p: Worship of trees and plants: people revere trees or plants as holy and honor them in religious practice.

V1.7.1.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 611a; *Fb “træ” III 866a; Wimberly 156; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
V1.7.1.p: Sacred tree: a particular tree is regarded as holy and worshipped.

V1.7.1.1.p: Sacred oak: an oak tree is regarded as holy and worshipped.

V1.7.1.2.p: Sacred ash: an ash tree is regarded as holy and worshipped.

V1.7.1.3.p: Sacred yew: a yew tree is regarded as holy and worshipped.

V1.7.1.4.p: Sacred bo-tree: a bo-tree (the fig tree associated with the Buddha) is regarded as holy and worshipped.

V1.8.p: Worship of animals: people revere certain animals as holy or divine and honor them in religious practice.

V1.8.1.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 142bc; **Burnell FL LVIII 377ff.; *Penzer II 240; Icelandic: Boberg.
V1.8.1.p: Cow worship: cows are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.1.1.p: Bull worship: bulls are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.2.p: Horse worship: horses are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.3.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 167b; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Werner 422.
V1.8.3.p: Dog worship: dogs are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 109, *Boberg.
V1.8.4.p: Swine worship: pigs or hogs are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.5.p: Wolf worship: wolves are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.6.p: Serpent worship: snakes are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.7.r: (Cf. A132.6.1.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 313f.
V1.8.7.p: Bird worship: birds are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.8.r: Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 103f.
V1.8.8.p: Dragon worship: dragons are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.9.p: Lion worship: lions are revered as holy and honored in religious practice.

V1.8.10.p: Worship of an ass, meaning a donkey treated as a sacred object of religious honor.

V1.8.11.p: Worship of fish, meaning fish treated as objects of religious veneration.

V1.9.p: Worship of tools and implements, meaning everyday tools being treated as sacred objects of religious honor.

V1.9.1.p: Worship of a plow, meaning a plow treated as a sacred object of religious honor.

V1.9.2.p: Worship of weapons, meaning weapons treated as sacred objects of religious honor.

V1.9.3.p: Worship of a hammer or axe, meaning such a tool treated as a sacred object of religious honor.

V1.10.r: (Cf. D1274.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 200a; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 96.
V1.10.p: Worship of a fetish, meaning an object believed to hold magical or spiritual power and treated as divine.

V1.10.1.p: A man worships a cake, and from time to time he eats it.

V1.10.2.p: Veneration of heads, meaning human heads kept and treated as sacred objects of worship.

V1.10.3.p: A feather regarded as sacred and treated as a holy object.

V1.11.p: Worship of idols, meaning man-made images or statues treated as gods.

V1.11.1.p: Worship of a golden calf, meaning a statue of a calf made of gold treated as a god.

V1.11.2.p: Worship of stone idols, meaning statues carved from stone treated as gods.

V1.11.3.p: Worship of a wooden idol, meaning a statue carved from wood treated as a god.

V4.p: The value or worth of religious observances, such as prayers and services, and how they are measured.

V4.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 465; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 65, 113, Beal XXI 325, 335.
V4.1.p: A son doubts that words spoken by priests are worth the money his father left them, but the words written on paper are found to outweigh the money.

V5.p: Neglect or carelessness in performing religious duties.

V5.1.p: The Virgin Mary scolds a monk who falls asleep at the altar.

V5.2.p: Negligent priests are buried under bags full of words they left out of the service.

V5.3.p: Devils make a monk sweat so that he stays away from church service.

V10.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 511b; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 19—54, 496—547; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 329; Jewish: *Neuman.
V10.p: Religious sacrifices in general: offerings made to gods, spirits or other powers as part of worship.

V10.1.p: A goddess stops a man from killing himself when he despairs because he cannot afford the sacrifice he must make.

V10.2.p: God rejects an offering that is more than a person can afford to give.

V11.p: The being or power to whom a sacrifice is offered, such as a tree, sea, stone, god or the dead.

V11.1.r: (Cf. V1.1.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 611a; Fb “træ” III 866a.
V11.1.p: A sacrifice is offered to a tree.

V11.2.r: *Penzer II 72 n. 1, VII 146 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
V11.2.p: A sacrifice is offered to the sea.

V11.2.1.p: A sacrifice is offered to a river, a kind of sea-sacrifice.

V11.3.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 570; *Fb “sten” III 553a; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 225, *Boberg; Danish: Schmidt DF XXXIX 90ff.
V11.3.p: A sacrifice is offered to a stone.

V11.4.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics IV 13f.; Chinese: Werner 102.

V11.5.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 645b; Icelandic: *Boberg; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 307 No. 29; Greek: Euripides Iphigenia at Aulis.
V11.5.p: A sacrifice is offered to the wind.

V11.6.r: (Cf. A108.1.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 512b; Irish myth: *Cross.
V11.6.p: A sacrifice is offered to the dead, usually ancestors or departed people.

V11.6.1.p: A human is sacrificed at a funeral.

V11.6.2.p: An animal is sacrificed at a funeral.

V11.7.p: A sacrifice is offered to an animal.

V11.7.1.p: A sacrifice is offered to a serpent or snake.

V11.8.p: A sacrifice is offered to a saint.

V11.9.p: A sacrifice is offered to a deity or god.

V11.9.1.p: A sacrifice is offered to a god that is not known or named.

V11.10.p: A sacrifice is offered to idols, that is, statues or images of gods.

V12.p: What kind of thing is offered in a sacrifice, such as the nature or type of the offering.

V12.1.p: Blood is offered as a sacrifice to a god or spirit.

V12.2.p: Jewels are thrown into the sea as an offering to the sea.

V12.3.p: Skulls are offered as a sacrifice to a god.

V12.4.p: Animals are killed and offered to a god or spirit as a sacrifice.

V12.4.0.1.p: Animals are sacrificed when a temple is built, to consecrate it.

V12.4.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 218 No. 167.
V12.4.1.p: A dog is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.2.p: A cat is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 218 No. 167.
V12.4.3.p: A pig is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.3.1.r: Icelandic: Boberg; Greek: Homer Odyssey XIV 435; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 123.
V12.4.3.1.p: A hog is offered as a sacrifice, another name for the pig motif.

V12.4.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg: Greek: Homer passim; Jewish: Neuman.
V12.4.4.p: An ox or bull is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.4.1.p: A cow is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.4.1.1.p: A heifer, a young cow, is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.4.2.p: A calf is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.5.p: A goat is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.6.p: A sheep or ram is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.7.p: A hare is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.8.p: A donkey or ass is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.9.p: A horse is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.10.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 19, 420; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 241.
V12.4.10.p: A fish is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.4.11.p: A bird is offered as a sacrifice.

V12.5.p: Gold is offered as a sacrifice to a false wooden idol or god.

V12.6.p: A person held in slavery or bondage is offered up as a sacrifice.

V12.7.p: Eyes, whether human or animal, are offered up as a sacrifice.

V12.8.p: Flowers are offered up as a sacrifice.

V12.9.p: A drink is poured out on the ground as an offering to the gods.

V12.10.p: Incense is burned as a sacrifice.

V13.p: A sacrifice is made when someone finds a treasure.

V14.p: A sacrificial animal or offering must be perfect, with no flaws or defects.

V15.p: An olive branch is laid on the altar of Mercy as a sacrifice.

V16.p: Sacrifices are made at religious festivals.

V16.1.p: Sacrifices are made during the Passover festival.

V17.p: Sacrifice is made for a particular purpose or reason.

V17.0.1.p: A sacrifice is made to a deity to obtain favors or blessings.

V17.1.p: A sacrifice is made to ensure a good year and good crops.

V17.2.p: A sacrifice is made to atone after committing a sin.

V17.3.p: A sacrifice is made to get help when in danger.

V17.4.p: A sacrifice is made to bring good weather.

V17.4.1.p: A sacrifice is made to bring snow and good conditions for skiing.

V17.5.p: A sacrifice is made to gain knowledge or secret information.

V17.5.1.p: A sacrifice is made to learn where an abducted daughter is being held.

V17.6.p: A sacrifice is offered so that the king will live for three hundred years.

V17.7.p: A sacrifice is made to a god to get back people who have been carried off.

V17.8.p: A sacrifice is offered when a temple is built or completed.

V17.9.p: Women make a sacrifice at the time of giving birth.

V18.p: A description of how a sacrifice is carried out as a ritual ceremony.

V19.p: A grouping of religious sacrifice motifs that do not fit under the other headings.

V19.1.p: Smoke rising from a sacrifice shows that the god has accepted it.

V20.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 133b; *De Vooys Middelnederlandse Legenden en Exempelen (Den Haag, 1926) 241ff.; *R. Pettazzoni La confessione dei peccati (Bologna, 1929); Jewish: *Neuman; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 143.
V20.p: Admitting one's sins to a religious person, such as a priest, as part of religious practice.

V20.1.r: *Crane Vitry 245 No. 261, 246f. No. 263; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V20.1.p: Sinners are kept safe or protected from harm because they have confessed.

V20.1.1.p: A person who has no confessor is said to be like a body without a head, meaning lost or incomplete without spiritual guidance.

V20.1.2.p: A confessor is called a soul-friend, a trusted spiritual adviser who hears confessions.

V21.r: Nouvelles de Sens No. 15; Spanish: Keller, Espinosa Jr. No. 182.
V21.p: Confessing a sin brings forgiveness for it.

V21.1.r: *Crane Vitry 266f. Nos. 301, 302; Alphabet Nos. 205, 209; Scala Celi 44b, 46a, 55a, 56b, 85b, 104a Nos. 251, 258, 308, 316, 493, 561; Ward II 663 No. 12; Herbert III 259, 380, 432, 469.
V21.1.p: A sincere confession is miraculously erased from the written record as a sign that the sin is forgiven.

V21.2.r: Alphabet No. 466; Scala Celi 47a No. 265; Wright Latin Stories 66.
V21.2.p: A woman who confesses to murder is not harmed when she is put to be burned, because her confession has forgiven her.

V21.3.p: A monk who planned to rob his monastery confesses and is forgiven, and later becomes prior.

V21.4.p: A prior forgives a friar who sinned, because the friar has confessed.

V21.5.p: A sinner confesses before committing the sin and is therefore pardoned for it.

V21.6.p: A bishop pardons a sinner's sins because the written confession is stained with the sinner's tears.

V22.r: (Cf. Q223.4.) Alphabet Nos. 231, 455; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 89 No. 760A*, Keller.
V22.p: A person is condemned for dying without having confessed.

V23.p: A miracle makes it possible for someone to confess.

V23.1.r: (Cf. V251.) Herbert III 14; *Crane Vitry 267 No. 303; *Crane Miraculis 93 No. 27; English: Wells 167 (Vernon Miracles).
V23.1.p: A man who died without confessing his sins is brought back to life so he can make his confession before dying for good.

V23.2.p: A mute man miraculously regains his speech so that he can confess his sins.

V24.p: A miracle happens during or because of a confession of sins.

V24.1.p: A pilgrim's confession of his sins at sea calms a violent storm.

V25.p: A confession that is made too easily, without real repentance, does not bring forgiveness.

V25.1.p: A dead man comes back to complain that the priest was too lenient with him when he confessed.

V25.2.p: A person who confesses a sin but refuses to give it up is punished anyway.

V27.p: A penance imposed for sin is ended or lifted through the act of confession.

V29.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about confession of sins that do not fit the other categories.

V29.1.r: Finally he succeeds. *Type 756C; **Andrejev FFC LIV 28ff.; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 46, 48, Beal XXI 317.
V29.1.p: A great sinner is sent from one confessor to another, and each refuses him, saying his sins are too great to be forgiven.

V29.2.p: Monks confess their own sins thoroughly because a brother possessed by a demon threatens to reveal all their sins.

V29.3.p: A miracle shows that a man has no need to confess, for example by hanging his sack on a sunbeam.

V29.4.p: A man who practices sodomy mocks the practice of confession.

V29.5.p: A husband does not need to confess because his wife has already confessed for him.

V29.6.p: A penitent brings a written list of his sins to confession.

V29.6.1.p: A written list of sins is miraculously cleansed, so that the penitent's sins are wiped away along with the paper.

V29.7.p: A confessor and a penitent trade confidences, balancing each other's sins and canceling wrongs done between them.

V29.8.p: The devil goes to confession. He does very harsh penance but cannot bring himself to humble himself before the altar.

V29.9.p: A greedy confessor demands a golden statue as the price of absolution.

V30.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 510; DeVooys Middelnederlandse Legenden en Exempelen (Den Haag, 1926) 230ff.; Irish myth: *Cross.
V30.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about the sacrament, a sacred rite of the church.

V30.1.p: A god is eaten, meaning a sacred being is consumed as food in a ritual or story.

V30.1.1.p: The flesh of the god Artemis is eaten in the form of a quail or a bear instead of as the sacred meal itself. The god is thus eaten in disguised animal form.

V31.p: A consecrated communion wafer is treated as unholy, meaning the host has not been properly blessed or made sacred. This heading introduces the stories grouped under it.

V31.1.r: Alphabet Nos 689, 691; Scala Celi 40b, 41a Nos. 229—36; Herbert III 398, 399, 465, 480, 483, 609, 709; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 409; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
V31.1.p: A sinful priest is judged unworthy, and the host is taken away from him so he cannot give it out.

V31.2.p: An unblessed host has no effect; it does not work its usual power on the person who takes it.

V31.3.p: A host that was not consecrated is refused, so the person who offers it or receives it is turned away or rejected.

V31.4.p: An altar rejects a host that has a louse baked into it, throwing the bread away rather than keeping it on the altar.

V31.5.p: The devil eats bread that has not been blessed, showing it has no sacred power to keep him away.

V32.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 129; Alphabet Nos. 160, 420; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Icelandic: Boberg.
V32.p: A priest refuses to give communion to a man, but a host miraculously comes to him anyway, showing God's will against the priest's decision.

V33.p: A person who doubts that the host is holy is punished for that disbelief.

V33.1.p: A person who doubts the holiness of the host is shown a miracle that proves it is sacred, which silences the doubt.

V33.1.1.p: A doubter who thinks the host does not really change into Christ's body and blood is convinced when Jesus's actual body and blood appear to him.

V34.p: The consecrated host works wonders, showing its miraculous power in healing, protection, or other effects.

V34.1.p: The consecrated host heals a sick person, curing their illness.

V34.2.p: A princess becomes ill because a toad has swallowed her consecrated wafer.

V34.3.p: A man who has received the sacrament overcomes an enemy who is a blasphemer, gaining power from the holy communion.

V34.4.p: A knight kneels in mud before the host as it passes, yet his clothes miraculously stay clean.

V35.p: Someone steals the consecrated host, and the theft leads to strange or miraculous events. This heading introduces such stories.

V35.1.p: Jews pay a woman to steal a host for them, and miraculous events follow the theft.

V35.1.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 556; Mensa Philosophica No. 59; Scala Celi 64a Nos. 349f.
V35.1.1.p: A horse kneels before the stolen sacrament, showing reverence for the holy host.

V35.1.2.p: A sacred image miraculously appears on the stolen sacrament, revealing its holiness.

V35.2.r: (Cf. C55, D1031.1.1.) Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 628ff.
V35.2.p: Stolen consecrated communion wafers are hidden in a coffin. Before she dies, a woman asks for a bag to be placed in her coffin, and the bag is found to be full of the stolen hosts.

V39.p: A grouping of miscellaneous tales about the Christian sacrament of Communion, the consecrated bread and wine taken in worship.

V39.1.p: A man believes he is too unworthy to receive communion, but God himself comes and gives him the host.

V39.2.p: A wicked woman cannot bear to be in the presence of the consecrated host during mass.

V39.3.r: Alphabet No. 687; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 126, Beal XXI 334, 337.
V39.3.p: Communion works even when given by a priest who is unworthy. A man who refused such a sacrament is shown in a vision a leper giving men good water without harm.

V39.4.r: Alphabet No. 694; Scala Celi 66a Nos. 360—64; Toldo IV 49ff.; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 109.
V39.4.p: A person sees the sacrament in a vision in the form of a small child.

V39.5.p: A sacred image appears on the consecrated host. The reward goes to a woman who vowed to wear no make-up or ornaments.

V39.6.p: A consecrated host is given as a pledge to guarantee that someone will keep his word.

V39.7.p: A voice from a grave asks for the coffin to be opened. The corpse spits out the host because he missed confession.

V39.8.p: Sick men die and go to hell because they hesitate to receive the sacrament before death.

V39.9.p: A woman who has eaten before taking communion cannot swallow the communion wafer.

V40.p: The Catholic or Christian Mass, the formal church service centered on the Eucharist.

V41.p: Masses, the church services, perform miracles and bring help to people in need.

V41.1.r: Ward II 675; Herbert III *85, 284, 324, 365; Alphabet No. 499.
V41.1.p: A miner trapped underground is kept alive by masses his wife has had said for him.

V41.2.r: *Liebrecht 29; Alphabet No. 462; Scala Celi 130b No. 714; *Ward II 662; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V41.2.p: A knight wins a tournament because masses were heard for him. An angel takes his place in the contest, and the absent knight is delayed by going to mass.

V42.r: Herbert III 284 Nos. 54ff. passim, 473; Alphabet Nos. 613, 652; Scala Celi 111b No. 620; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 228; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 99, Beal XXI 332; English: Wells 172 (Trentalle Sancti Gregorii); Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 298 No. 11; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 192—97.
V42.p: Masses said for the dead free souls from hell or purgatory.

V43.r: (Cf. F1011.1, V29.3.) When upbraided for not coming to mass, he hangs his coat on a sunbeam. Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 309 No. 10; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 147 No. 1805B.
V43.p: A holy man is given his own private mass, celebrated especially for him.

V44.r: *Crane Vitry Nos. 223ff. passim; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 98, Beal XXI 331.
V44.p: Regularly attending mass is worth more than the person's evil deeds, so the faithful attender is saved despite sins.

V45.p: A mass is said for dead people, and they rise from their graves and say Amen.

V46.p: A pebble is put into a box each time a person hears mass, so the count of masses attended can be tallied.

V48.p: The set of fixed daily prayer times that the Church appoints for its members to pray at.

V49.p: A general heading for miscellaneous tale elements involving the Mass, the central Christian worship service.

V49.1.r: (Cf. D113.1.1, E492, G243.) Köhler-Bolte I 134; Gascon: Bladé Contes pop. de Gascogne II 360 No. 4.
V49.1.p: Werewolves are shown holding a Mass, the Christian church service.

V49.2.p: An angel takes the place of a priest and holds Mass in the church on the day the king is away on a hunting trip.

V50.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 470a; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
V50.p: A general heading for tale elements involving prayer, the act of addressing God or saints in worship or request.

V51.p: A general heading for tale elements about how people learn to pray, or pray well.

V51.1.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 332; **Andrejev “Tri Starca” Novoje Delo (Kazan, 1922) (see Anderson Zs. f. Vksk. XXX-XXXII 171); Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 827*; Russian: Andrejev No. 827*.
V51.1.p: A man who does not know how to pray is so holy that he can walk on water.

V51.2.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 334, 338; Scala Celi 37b No. 209.
V51.2.p: People who are preoccupied with worldly concerns learn to pray by thinking about their usual work or business.

V51.3.p: A woman demonstrates that the Lord's Prayer is the best prayer.

V51.4.p: A woman is taught that it is better to pray before an image of Christ than before an image of a saint.

V51.5.p: The prayer Beatus is held to be the best prayer for rescuing condemned souls.

V52.r: Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 334, O’Suilleabhain 112; Spanish Exempla: Keller; West Indies: Flowers 579. Cf. Nouvelles de Sens No. 26.
V52.p: A general heading for tales in which prayer works miracles.

V52.1.p: A man is saved from lustful temptation through prayer.

V52.2.r: *Type 307; *BP III 534; *Köhler-Bolte II 213ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 313, 319, O’Suilleabhain 37, 53; Japanese: Ikeda.
V52.2.p: A man is kept alive through a frightful night-long watch by continuous praying.

V52.3.r: Scala Celi 151b No. 833; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V52.3.p: Prayer offered before a battle brings victory.

V52.4.p: Objects are provided by God in answer to prayer.

V52.5.p: A shattered vessel is restored whole through prayer.

V52.6.p: Sailors are rescued from a whirlpool or maelstrom through prayer.

V52.7.p: Praying at a saint's flagstone prevents harm or misfortune.

V52.8.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 105, 345.
V52.8.p: A prayer causes the death of an enemy.

V52.9.p: A person praying for safe passage on a journey to the land of the dead is protected along the way.

V52.10.p: A devout woman's prayers free her husband from death and from imprisonment.

V52.11.p: A sinner's prayer turns his skin from black to white.

V52.12.p: Two brothers work hard and grow rich, while the foolish third brother only prays, yet in the end he gets all the property.

V52.13.p: A saint's Paternoster (Lord's Prayer) is so heavy that it outweighs an ox on a scale.

V52.14.p: Reciting the martyrology (list of saints' deaths) keeps the body of the reciter from decaying after death.

V52.15.p: A saint says a prayer into his right hand and uses it to put back an opponent's eye that was knocked out of its socket.

V53.p: Family members pray together to comfort and support a person held in prison.

V53.1.p: A boy's fetters (shackles) are unfastened through prayer.

V55.p: A man worships a devil's image to gain promotion or success.

V57.p: The reasons for which people pray, as told in folk narratives.

V57.1.p: A prayer asking for a good harvest of crops.

V57.2.p: A prayer asking for a shower of gold to fall from heaven.

V57.3.p: Prayers said on special occasions, such as festivals or important events.

V58.p: Prayer performed as a set ritual or ceremony rather than spontaneously.

V58.1.p: Prayers offered at sunrise and at sunset.

V58.2.p: A person prays while facing east.

V58.3.p: A person walks around something repeatedly while praying.

V58.4.p: A person washes their hands before praying.

V59.p: A general heading for stories in which a prayer is answered in some unspecified or miscellaneous way.

V59.1.p: A person asks for prayer help and is granted skill at stealing.

V60.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 212a; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
V60.p: A general heading for the ceremonies and customs performed for the dead.

V60.1.p: Stones are sold to people at funeral wakes.

V60.2.p: Druids perform the funeral rites for the dead.

V61.p: A general heading for the different ways that the dead are disposed of, such as burial, burning, or placing on a boat.

V61.1.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 79c, 545b; Fb “skib” III 243b; Icelandic: *Boberg. Cf. Beowulf.
V61.1.p: The dead body is laid on a boat, usually for it to be carried away or set adrift.

V61.2.r: (Cremation.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 143c; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
V61.2.p: The dead body is burned on a funeral pyre.

V61.3.p: The coffin or body is buried standing upright rather than lying down.

V61.3.0.1.p: A hero is buried standing upright in armor, facing toward the land of his enemies.

V61.3.0.2.p: A person is buried standing upright with friends gathered around him.

V61.3.0.3.p: A man is buried upright beneath the kitchen stairway so that he can keep watch over his family.

V61.4.p: The head and the body of the dead person are buried in two different places.

V61.4.1.p: The corpse is buried lying face down.

V61.4.2.p: The body is cut into pieces before it is buried.

V61.5.p: A king is buried together with his war chariot.

V61.6.p: A Christian is buried in a coffin made of stone.

V61.7.p: A Christian is buried in a coffin made of wood.

V61.8.p: The dead are buried inside a grave-mound, a raised earth or stone burial heap.

V61.8.1.p: Chiefs are buried in caves that have been hidden away so no one can find them.

V61.9.p: A lion is buried in a stone cave inscribed with gold letters.

V61.10.p: Dead bodies are left up in a tree instead of being buried in the ground.

V61.11.p: A person refuses to be buried in a foreign or unfamiliar city and wants to be laid to rest elsewhere.

V62.p: Rules or prohibitions that limit or forbid the ordinary burial of the dead.

V62.1.p: Someone forbids any funeral rites from being performed for the dead person.

V62.2.p: Only usurers, moneylenders who charge illegal interest, are allowed to carry a usurer's body to the grave.

V63.p: The bones of a person who was cut into pieces are gathered together and buried.

V64.p: Money is tied to a corpse that is thrown overboard from a ship so the dead person will get a proper burial.

V64.1.p: Shipwrecked people each receive a piece of the chief's gold ring so that they will have gold with them in death.

V65.p: Ways of remembering and honoring someone after they have died.

V65.1.p: Calves are kept apart from cows as a memorial to a hero's death.

V65.2.p: A drinking festival is held to remember the dead.

V65.3.p: A wedding and a funeral festival are held at the same time.

V65.4.r: Virgil Aeneid XI 37; Greek: Aeschylus Libation-Pourers 423; India: Thompson-Balys.
V65.4.p: Hired people are paid to mourn and wail for the dead.

V65.4.1.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. VIII 1071ff.; *E. Reiner Die rituelle Totenklage der Griechen (Stuttgart, 1938); Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
V65.4.1.p: A funeral song is sung over the dead person by professional mourners.

V65.5.p: Games and contests are held in honor of the dead at their funeral.

V66.p: A speech or sermon given at a funeral.

V66.1.p: A funeral sermon that damns the dead man with faint praise or tells anecdotes with unflattering implications, because the priest has nothing good to say about him.

V67.p: Things that are placed with the body or done along with a burial.

V67.1.p: Weapons, chariots, or other ornaments are buried together with a hero.

V67.2.p: The dead are buried with shoes placed in the grave with them.

V67.3.p: Treasure is buried in the grave along with the dead person.

V67.3.1.r: *Krappe “Les funérailles d’Alaric” Annuaire de l’institut de philologie et d’histoire orientales et slaves VII 229—40.
V67.3.1.p: A king is buried with great treasure in the bed of a river that has been artificially drained for the purpose; afterward the river is made to flow in its normal course again.

V67.4.p: Men are killed and buried with their dead chief or leader so they can serve him in the afterlife.

V67.4.1.p: A ship's captain is buried together with his crew.

V67.5.p: Animals are buried along with the dead person.

V68.p: Various steps taken to prepare a dead body before it is buried.

V68.1.p: The dead body is washed in a river before burial.

V68.2.p: The dead body is washed and its hair is combed before burial.

V68.3.p: A dying hero asks to be buried in the clothes of his brother, who has just killed him.

V68.4.p: The dead body is stripped of its clothing.

V68.4.1.p: The dead must not be buried without clothing.

V68.5.p: The dead body is rubbed with red paint before burial.

V69.p: Miscellaneous funeral customs that do not fit other categories.

V69.1.p: All the dead from a battle are given burial afterward.

V69.2.p: A hero is buried under the guise of an unknown merchant in a foreign land.

V70.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 198; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
V70.p: Religious holy days on which feasting or fasting is observed.

V70.1.p: Festivals held on the first day of summer.

V70.1.1.p: The Beltane festival, held on May Day, marks the start of summer.

V70.2.p: The festival of Whitsuntide, the Christian feast of Pentecost celebrated seven weeks after Easter.

V70.3.p: Midsummer, the summer solstice festival, kept as a religious feast or observance.

V70.3.1.p: A religious feast held in honor of Saint John the Baptist, celebrated as part of the Midsummer observances.

V70.4.p: A religious festival held to celebrate the harvest.

V70.5.p: The Samhain festival, a Celtic-linked feast at the turn of autumn into winter, associated with Hallowe'en and with the site of Tara.

V70.6.p: The Imbolg festival, a Celtic-linked feast associated with Saint Brigit and Candlemas, held in early February.

V70.7.p: A feast held at the new moon as a religious observance.

V70.8.p: A festival held in honor of Cenn Cruaich, also called Crom Cruaich, a pagan Irish idol or deity.

V71.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 509c; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Moreno Esdras (V71.2.), *Neuman.
V71.p: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest and religious observance, and the rules and events connected with keeping it.

V71.1.p: A Jewish automaton, or mechanical servant, that stops working on Saturday, the Sabbath.

V71.1.1.p: Manna, the food that fell from heaven for the Israelites, does not fall on the Sabbath.

V71.2.p: Someone suffers misfortune because they broke the Sabbath by working or otherwise violating its rest.

V71.3.p: A range of events, from the Creation to the Resurrection, are said to have happened on the Sabbath.

V72.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 121b; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX 979ff., IX Nachträge 864—968; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
V72.p: Christmas, the feast celebrating the birth of Christ, and customs and tales connected with it.

V72.1.p: Little Christmas, a festive observance held shortly after Christmas, traditionally around Epiphany.

V73.p: Periods of fasting, going without food as a religious discipline or for some other purpose.

V73.0.1.p: Christ resists the devil in the wilderness by fasting, and so overcomes him.

V73.1.p: A fast is kept to prevent a plague or epidemic from spreading.

V73.2.p: Fasting is believed to improve a person's health.

V73.3.p: A saint has two young men fed the best food, then declares one is damned to hell and the other will become an ascetic in old age.

V73.4.p: A person fasts to ensure a safe and successful journey.

V73.5.p: People fast on Fridays that fall on a special day called the Golden Friday, believing this protects them from certain misfortunes.

V73.6.p: Lent, the period of fasting before Easter observed by Christians.

V73.6.1.p: Christ's forty days of fasting in the wilderness are called "His Lent" in the tale.

V73.6.2.p: A saint keeps silent throughout Lent by holding a stone in his mouth.

V73.6.3.p: A holy man during Lent eats pork and beef, reasoning that pigs are fed on milk and oxen on grass, but refuses cake because it contains weevils, which are living creatures and so count as meat.

V75.p: Easter, the Christian spring festival celebrating Christ's resurrection.

V75.1.p: Passover, the Jewish spring festival commemorating the exodus from Egypt, appears in the tale.

V80.p: Miscellaneous religious services and rites not covered by other headings.

V81.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 61c; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 337, O’Suilleabhain 128; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
V81.p: Baptism, the Christian rite of admitting someone into the church with water.

V81.1.p: A girl who has been stolen by mountain people must be baptized again before she can return to normal human life.

V81.2.p: Mountain spirits lose their tails when they are baptized.

V81.3.p: Baptism changes a creature's form. A monster born from a heathen ruler and a Christian maiden becomes a handsome boy once baptized.

V81.4.p: Infants are baptized as babies in the Christian custom.

V81.5.r: Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 144; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 152, 176.
V81.5.p: A bath in the sea is used as a ritual of purification, taking the place of baptism.

V82.r: (Cf. F81.3.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 126c; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V82.p: Circumcision, the ritual removal of the foreskin, as a religious rite.

V83.p: Hymns, religious songs sung in worship.

V84.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 193b; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V84.p: Excommunication, the church's formal expulsion of a person from its community and sacraments.

V84.1.p: A person who has been excommunicated is struck by lightning when they enter a church.

V84.2.r: Scala Celi 85b No. 495; Herbert III 446 No. 17.
V84.2.p: A priest demonstrates the power of excommunication by using the consecrated host, which turns black.

V84.3.p: An excommunicated pirate goes on a pilgrimage as penance to be readmitted to the church.

V85.p: People travel to sacred places as a religious act, making pilgrimages to shrines or holy sites.

V86.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics VI 539b; Fb “kors” II 274; Scala Celi 67b—71b Nos. 373—404 passim.
V86.p: Making the sign of the cross, tracing a cross over oneself or an object, as a religious gesture.

V86.1.p: Making the sign of the cross keeps a person or thing from being harmed.

V86.1.1.p: Making the sign of the cross over a cradle keeps a baby from being stolen, often by fairies or evil beings.

V86.1.2.p: Making the sign of the cross over a piece of clothing keeps it from catching fire.

V86.1.3.p: A man who kills someone while the victim bears a sign of the cross on the forehead dies as a result.

V86.2.r: (Cf. V254.3.) Herbert III 77, 416, 467, 487, 530; Scala Celi 69b No. 388; Alphabet No. 563.
V86.2.p: A martyr is found with a sign of the cross marked on his heart.

V86.3.p: Someone who uses the cross irreverently, such as a drunkard who kisses a cross thinking it is a bottle of wine, is punished.

V86.4.r: Alphabet. No. 230; English: Wells 97 (Chevalere Assigne), 89 (The Sege of Melayne).
V86.4.p: Scoffers who mock the cross are shown miraculous signs or manifestations as a warning or punishment.

V86.5.p: A person prays with outstretched arms so that the body forms the shape of a cross.

V86.6.p: A loaf of bread bursts in the oven because no sign of the cross was made over it before baking.

V86.7.p: A teaching or account listing seven meanings or symbolic significances of making the sign of the cross.

V87.p: The ceremony of baptizing a child or person into the Christian faith, giving them a name.

V88.p: A ceremony in which a Buddha is publicly proclaimed or announced.

V91.p: A person who accidentally calls on God's name is judged to be saved, even though they had lived a wicked life.

V92.r: *Herbert III 417; *Wicksteed Romania II 315; Romanische Forschungen XI 223.
V92.p: A tumbler who became a monk dances before an image of the Virgin while others chant psalms, honoring God in the only way he knows.

V93.p: Dancing performed as an act of worship or as part of a religious service.

V96.p: Bathing performed as a religious rite of purification.

V96.1.p: A ritual bath taken in the Ganges, a sacred river in India, to gain religious merit or purification.

V97.p: Studying the Torah, the Jewish sacred law and scripture, is treated as a religious service in itself.

V100.p: A general heading for sacred places and religious objects, such as buildings, shrines and holy items.

V110.p: A general heading for religious buildings such as churches, temples, shrines and sacred groves.

V111.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 123c; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 335, O’Suilleabhain 112.
V111.p: Churches as places of Christian worship that appear in tales.

V111.1.p: A traveler on a pilgrimage to a particular church is kept safe from drowning because of having visited it.

V111.2.r: (Cf. D931.0.1.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
V111.2.p: Stones needed to build a church or chapel appear by supernatural means without anyone bringing them.

V111.3.p: A supernatural sign shows where a church must be built.

V111.3.1.p: Birds show the site for a church by building a model of the church on the spot.

V111.3.2.p: A divine being points out the place where a church is to be built.

V112.p: Temples, the sacred buildings used for worship in various religions.

V112.0.1.p: The ark of the temple, the sacred chest kept in a temple.

V112.1.p: Small huts built as dwellings or shrines for spirits.

V112.2.p: Mosques, the Muslim houses of worship.

V112.3.p: Synagogues, the Jewish houses of worship.

V113.r: (Cf. C51.1.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 546a; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman.
V113.p: Shrines, small sacred places where people pray or leave offerings to a holy figure.

V113.0.1.p: Miraculous events that happen at a shrine.

V113.0.2.p: A person promises to visit a shrine, usually in return for help or safety.

V113.1.p: Crippled people at a shrine are so frightened that they run off without their crutches.

V113.2.p: Robbers promise to give offerings to a hermit's shrine if their robbery succeeds.

V114.r: *Frazer Golden Bough XII 293 s.v. “Grove(s), sacred”; Irish myth: *Cross.
V114.p: Sacred groves, small wooded areas regarded as holy.

V114.1.p: Sacred groves belonging to the druids, the priests of the ancient Celts.

V115.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 69a; Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 868ff.; E. Lippert Glockenläuten als Rechtsbrauch (Freiburg im Breisgau, 1939); *P. Sartori Das Buch von deutschen Glocken (Berlin, 1932).—Irish myth: *Cross; Norwegian: Solheim Register 21.
V115.p: Church bells as a theme or object in folk narratives. Thompson lists this as the heading for the bell motifs that follow.

V115.1.r: (Cf. F993.) *Fb. “kirkeklokke” IV 260b; Wales, England: *Baughman; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 47 No. 88; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 72 Nos. 608—11; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 135 No. 88.
V115.1.p: A church bell falls into a river or the sea and sinks. The stories then tell what happens to it afterward.

V115.1.1.p: After sinking, the bell keeps moving along the bottom of the sea, so it is not found in one place.

V115.1.2.p: People try to bring a sunken church bell back up out of the water, and the story tells how this is done.

V115.1.3.p: A sunken church bell cannot be lifted out of the water, however people try.

V115.1.3.1.p: The sunken bell cannot be raised because someone breaks the silence or quiet that the situation requires.

V115.1.3.2.p: The sunken bell cannot be raised because someone swears or speaks blasphemously.

V115.2.p: A girl is sold in exchange for a new church bell.

V115.3.p: The devil buys a church bell and so upsets the congregation. Since they had no bell to tell the time, they used to come to church early; now they wait for the bell to ring.

V115.4.p: Stories in which church bells are said to speak, giving a message in their ringing or tolling.

V116.r: (Cf. V135.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 18a; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
V116.p: Altars as a religious object in folk narratives. Thompson uses this heading for the altar motifs under it.

V117.p: Pulpits as a religious object in folk narratives. Thompson uses this heading for the pulpit motifs under it.

V118.p: Monasteries as a place in folk narratives. Thompson uses this heading for the monastery motifs under it.

V118.0.1.p: Hell is pictured as a monastery, with the devil as abbot and sinners as the monks.

V118.1.p: A monastery stands on an island in the otherworld, the supernatural realm beyond ordinary life.

V118.2.p: A monastery lies underwater beneath a lake or sea.

V118.2.1.p: A small chapel for prayer lies under the sea, as part of a submerged monastery.

V120.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 271b; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
V120.p: Religious images, such as statues or pictures of holy figures, as they appear in folk narratives. Thompson uses this heading for the image motifs under it.

V120.1.p: Religious images appear together with druids, the priests of the ancient Celtic religion.

V121.p: An image of Christ miraculously appears imprinted on a cloth, such as a napkin or towel.

V122.p: A nun tries to flee her convent to be with her lover, but a religious image blocks her way.

V122.1.p: A figure of Jesus comes down from the cross and wounds a nun who is trying to leave the convent.

V123.r: Type 1479**, *Wesselski Arlotto I 196 No. 23; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
V123.p: A person who prays to a religious image blames it for his misfortunes.

V123.1.p: A petitioner forces God's hand by threatening to mutilate or crush a holy image unless his wish is granted.

V124.p: A preacher criticizes the picture of Christ displayed in his church, saying it does not do the original justice.

V124.1.p: A saint hangs a monk's hood on a thornbush as a symbol of Christ on the cross.

V125.p: A Buddha statue cannot be cast until a madman's small coin is thrown into the furnace.

V126.p: A statue or picture of a saint speaks.

V127.r: (Cf. V1.11.) Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 111; Cook Islands: ibid. 131; Marquesas: Handy 122; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 344.
V127.p: A god is represented by an image carved in wood or stone.

V128.p: Various movements or actions are credited to religious images.

V128.1.p: An apple is offered to a statue of the Virgin and Child, and the infant reaches out and takes the fruit.

V128.2.p: Portraits or pictures of holy figures give off oil.

V130.p: Other sacred objects used in worship.

V131.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 629c; Gaster Thespis 270f.; Jewish: *Neuman.
V131.p: Sacred garments worn by religious officials.

V131.1.p: Seeing a sacred fringe on a garment stops a man from committing fornication and reforms a prostitute.

V131.2.p: Druids are described as wearing white robes.

V132.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics IV 61f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
V132.p: Holy water, water blessed for religious use.

V132.1.p: Holy water keeps a man from committing incest with his daughter.

V132.2.1.p: Holy water washes away a mark the devil put on a man's face.

V132.3.p: Drinking holy water gives a person the power to curse others effectively.

V133.p: Holy candles are treated as sacred objects with special powers in religious practice.

V134.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 640c; Fb “kilde” II 119: Namn och Bygd XXXIII (1945) 1ff. — Danish: Schmidt Danmarks Helligkilder (DF XXXIII); Irish myth: *Cross; England, Wales, Ireland, U.S.: Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg.
V134.p: Sacred wells are springs or pools regarded as holy, with religious significance and power.

V134.0.1.p: A tree grows beside a holy well and shares in its sanctity.

V134.1.p: Omens, predictions, or answers to questions are obtained from a holy well.

V134.2.p: People leave gifts or offerings at holy wells.

V134.3.p: A fish taken from a certain well causes the water to refuse to boil until the fish is returned to the well.

V134.4.p: Ducks kept in a church pool cause water in which they are cooked to refuse to boil until they are put back in the pool.

V135.p: Altar cloths are sacred church coverings with special significance in religious tales.

V135.1.p: A poor couple wraps their newborn baby in altar coverings because they have nothing else.

V136.p: The Bible is treated as a sacred object with special powers or significance in tales.

V136.1.p: A copy of the Gospels is buried together with a saint.

V137.p: A woman who washes clothes for the church is spared when a great fire destroys the town, her house being protected because of her service.

V140.r: **Saintyves Les réliques et les images légendaires (Paris, 1912); Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 493a.
V140.p: Sacred relics are the bodily remains or belongings of holy people, treated as objects of religious power.

V140.1.p: An angel shows a saint where relics have been buried.

V140.2.p: A saint's relics are recovered by miracle after being lost or hidden.

V140.3.p: A cow licks the stone under which a saint's body has been secretly buried, revealing the grave.

V140.4.p: To test whether bones are genuine relics, they are thrown into a fire, and genuine ones jump away from the flames with a loud noise.

V141.p: Owning a relic brings prosperity to its owner, while losing it brings sickness.

V142.p: A devout person who unknowingly owns fake relics is miraculously given genuine ones instead.

V142.1.p: A person who devoutly believes in fake relics is rewarded when the relics they hold become genuine and perform miracles.

V143.p: The bones of a saint leave their church on their own when people no longer honor the saint.

V143.1.p: The bones of a saint are miraculously removed from their reliquary, which was broken during a raid or looting.

V143.2.p: Sacred images that have been carried off return by themselves to the church they came from.

V144.p: The belief that sacred relics have miraculous powers.

V144.1.p: Sacred relics are carried into battle so that they will help the army win.

V144.2.p: The relics of a saint protect horses from being attacked by wild animals.

V150.p: A miscellaneous category of sacred objects that do not fit the other religious object groups.

V151.p: Sacred writings, such as holy texts, that have special power or significance in a story.

V151.1.p: A captive is freed because he is able to recite the opening passage of Genesis.

V200.1.p: A flame lights up the cradle of a holy person, showing that the child is sacred.

V201.p: God as a sacred being in religious belief and story.

V202.p: Holy or divine spirits that are sacred beings in religious belief.

V205.p: The belief that a royal family is sacred and holds special divine status.

V205.1.p: The third son of a king has sacred or supernatural power.

V210.p: Founders of religions, who are sacred figures in religious tradition and story.

V211.r: *DeVooys Middelnederlandse Legenden en Exempelen (Den Haag, 1926) 129ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V211.p: Christ, the central sacred figure of Christianity, as a character in religious stories.

V211.0.1.p: Christ is born from the crown of the Virgin Mary's head rather than in the usual way.

V211.0.2.p: Christ is conceived on the same day that he was crucified.

V211.0.3.p: Seventeen miraculous marvels are said to have occurred at the birth of Christ.

V211.0.4.p: Christ is regarded as a prophet, a messenger who foretells or speaks for God.

V211.0.5.p: Christ is called a "druid," a term for a priest-like wise man of the Celts.

V211.1.p: The birth of Christ, told as a motif in its own right.

V211.1.1.p: The air becomes sweet-smelling when Christ is born.

V211.1.2.p: A star shines brightly even during the daytime on the day Christ is born.

V211.1.2.1.p: A hairy comet, a star with a tail, appears before Christ's birth.

V211.1.3.p: A shining cloud shows the exact place where Christ was born.

V211.1.3.1.p: On the night of Christ's birth there is a vast light so bright it is almost unbearable to see.

V211.1.4.p: The Virgin Mary gives birth to Christ without any pain.

V211.1.5.p: At the moment of Christ's birth, all of nature is silent and still.

V211.1.6.p: Among the gifts the shepherds give to Joseph, husband of Mary, is a crown of thorns.

V211.1.7.p: Three (or seven) druids come to worship the infant Jesus.

V211.1.8.p: The infant Jesus appears as a child, as a motif in its own right.

V211.1.8.1.p: Christ appears as a baby being nursed by a saint.

V211.1.8.2.p: Christ appears as a baby being fondled and cuddled by nuns.

V211.1.8.3.p: While the infant Christ is held in his mother's arms, a bare hillside turns into a field of wheat to protect them.

V211.2.p: Christ's time on earth, told as a motif in its own right.

V211.2.1.p: A pillar of fire appears as a sign that Christ is visiting.

V211.2.1.1.p: Christ comes among people disguised as a leper.

V211.2.1.2.p: Christ comes among people disguised as a beggar.

V211.2.1.2.1.p: Christ, when he visits the earth in disguise, is described as having dark hair and a long red beard. This is a detail of how he appeared in the visit story.

V211.2.2.p: After Christ's visit to the earth ends, he leaves behind his bachall, the staff or crook associated with saints.

V211.2.3.p: Christ is crucified, nailed to the cross, on Calvary.

V211.2.3.0.1.p: An angel warns Christ that he is in danger before the crucifixion.

V211.2.3.0.2.p: A man named Smith's wife makes the nails used for the cross because her husband believes Christ is a true prophet.

V211.2.3.1.p: At the crucifixion of Christ, the earth shakes and trembles.

V211.2.3.2.p: At the crucifixion of Christ, the moon turns blood-red.

V211.2.3.3.p: At the crucifixion of Christ, the sun grows dark.

V211.3.p: The discovery of the true cross on which Christ was crucified.

V211.4.p: The making of the cross on which Christ was crucified.

V211.4.1.p: The cross of Christ is said to have been made from four different kinds of wood.

V211.5.p: The five wounds that Christ received at the crucifixion.

V211.5.1.p: When the crucified Savior's side is wounded, blood and wine flow out of the wound.

V211.6.p: A conversation between Christ and the Virgin Mary.

V211.7.p: Christ's journey down into hell after his death.

V211.7.1.p: Christ breaks into hell and releases the souls held there.

V211.7.2.p: During Christ's descent into hell, he and Satan argue or debate with each other.

V211.7.3.p: Christ leaves three bolts on the gates of hell, locking them shut.

V211.8.p: Christ rises from the dead, dated to March 27 in this tradition.

V211.9.p: Christ ascends bodily into Heaven, dated to May 5 in this tradition.

V211.10.r: Irish myth: *Cross. Cf. North Carolina: Brown Collection I 642.
V211.10.p: Christ sends a letter or written message to people. The letter itself is treated as a miraculous or sacred object.

V211.10.1.p: Christ sends a message to clerics (church officials) who are travelling by sea. The message reaches them while they are at sea.

V212.p: The Buddha, the founder of Buddhism, appears as a sacred figure in the tale.

V212.1.p: Someone receives sacred books directly from the Buddha himself, face to face.

V212.2.p: Someone hears moral rules or commandments (precepts) spoken directly by the Buddha in person.

V220.r: **Toldo Studien zur vgl. Litgsch. I—IX passim; **Saintyves Saints Successeurs 23—26; *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 514a.—Norwegian: Solheim Register 22; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 140—42, 162, 210, 411. For references in addition to those given below, see volume VI s.v. “Saints”.
V220.p: Saints, holy people honored by the church for their virtue, appear as sacred figures in the tale.

V221.r: Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 246a; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: *Boberg.
V221.p: A saint performs a miraculous healing, curing sickness or injury through holy power.

V221.0.1.p: The relics (sacred bodily remains or objects) of a saint cure disease when used or touched.

V221.0.1.1.p: Oil that flows from a saint's relics has healing powers and can cure people.

V221.0.1.2.p: Water or wine used to wash a saint's relics sometimes gains healing powers.

V221.0.1.3.p: A saint's shrine is carried in procession to stop a plague or epidemic.

V221.0.2.p: A saint is miraculously healed of an illness or injury.

V221.0.2.1.p: A saint who was crippled is miraculously given a horse and chariot, which allows him to get about.

V221.0.3.p: A saint shows healing power already as a child.

V221.1.p: A saint cures paralysis or palsy, restoring the use of a person's limbs.

V221.2.p: A saint restores the speech of a mute man, enabling him to speak again.

V221.3.p: A saint cures leprosy, the disease that was feared and caused skin sores and disfigurement.

V221.3.1.p: A leper is cured when a saint kisses him.

V221.4.p: A saint subdues or calms a violent madman, bringing him under control.

V221.4.0.1.p: A saint cures or calms an animal that has gone mad and is attacking, such as a frenzied beast.

V221.4.0.1.1.p: A saint's blessing is enough to calm a rabid dog that has gone mad. The saint cures a frenzied animal simply by blessing it.

V221.5.p: A saint makes a monk pure again by making the sign of the cross over him. The sign of the cross cleanses the monk.

V221.6.p: A saint keeps a man alive while he hangs on the gallows. The saint holds the condemned man up so the hanging does not kill him.

V221.7.p: A woman with an incurable illness is cured when she kisses a letter from a saint. The letter itself carries the healing power.

V221.8.p: Wounds that a saint has healed leave no scars behind. The cure is complete and the skin shows no mark.

V221.9.p: A saint reattaches body parts that have been cut off. The severed limb or part is joined back on to the body.

V221.10.p: A saint cures men who have an enormous and unnatural appetite. After the cure they no longer feel such hunger.

V221.11.p: A saint restores the speech of a person who cannot talk. The mute person is able to speak again.

V221.12.p: A saint restores sight to a blind person. The blind person can see after the saint's cure.

V222.r: Alphabet Nos. 345, 354, 602, 637, 762; Irish: Beal XXI 305, 326, 335, O’Suilleabhain 70f., 115; Spanish: Keller, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 45, 182; India: Thompson-Balys.
V222.p: A miraculous sign shows the public that a person is a saint. Wonders appear to announce the holiness of the saint.

V222.0.1.p: Visions of miracles foretell that a saint is about to be born. The future holiness of the child is shown before birth.

V222.0.1.1.p: A pillar of fire rises above a pregnant woman who will bear a saint. The fire signals the holiness of the child she carries.

V222.0.1.2.p: A saint is recognized as holy by a pillar of fire above her head. The fire identifies the saint.

V222.0.1.3.p: A dazzling heavenly light, shining both day and night, marks the place where a saint was born. The light shows the spot is holy.

V222.0.2.p: Angels appear above the place where a saint is born. Their presence announces the birth.

V222.1.r: Alphabet No. 473; Plummer cxxxviii, clxxviii; Loomis White Magic 27f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
V222.1.p: A marvelous light shines around a saint and accompanies them. The light is a sign of the saint's holiness.

V222.1.0.1.p: A supernaturally bright light shines over an infant saint while it sleeps. The light marks the child as holy.

V222.1.0.2.p: Heaven falls upon an infant saint in the form of a drop of light. The heavenly drop marks the child as holy.

V222.1.1.p: The church fills with radiant light when a saint dies. The brightness marks the saint's death.

V222.1.2.p: The hand of a saint becomes bright because the Lord touches it. The brightness is so intense that no mortal can look at it afterward.

V222.1.3.p: A column of light comes down from heaven onto a man chosen by God, marking him out as holy.

V222.1.4.p: Mysterious lights appear over the grave of a saint, showing where his body is buried.

V222.2.p: A saint loses a tooth into a brake (a thicket of bracken or brushwood), and the thicket suddenly catches fire.

V222.3.p: Choirs of singing are heard accompanying a saint, a sign of his holiness.

V222.4.p: The house of a saint becomes filled with a sweet fragrance.

V222.4.1.p: The body of a saint gives off a pleasant, spicy smell.

V222.5.p: When a saint is made a bishop, oil gushes up out of the ground.

V222.6.r: Irish myth: Cross; England: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
V222.6.p: A bell rings by itself when a saint is approaching.

V222.6.1.p: Church bells ring by themselves, with no one pulling the ropes, when a holy person dies.

V222.7.p: A dead holy man reaches a hand out of his tomb to pay honor to a saint.

V222.8.p: A holy man walks through fire because of his faith, and only his clothing burns.

V222.9.p: An earthquake occurs when a holy man enters the palace of a heathen emperor.

V222.10.p: A saint falls into a deep chasm but is found perched in the branches of a tree growing out of the cliff. Once he is pulled up, the tree disappears.

V222.11.p: Flowers fall from a saint's mouth whenever he speaks.

V222.12.p: A holy man makes a garden bloom again.

V222.13.p: The sun sends down a ray of heat that cooks meat given to a persecuted saint.

V222.14.p: Roses lose their thorns when a saint walks over them.

V222.15.p: A saint turns the maggots in a nun's sores into precious stones.

V222.16.p: Robbers who come into a saint's garden to steal are made to dig it over for him. This shows that he is a saint.

V223.r: Alphabet No. 482; *Loomis White Magic 72f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 307 No. 25.
V223.p: Saints have miraculous knowledge, knowing things they could not otherwise know.

V223.1.p: A saint gives wise advice to someone, drawing on knowledge he has by miracle.

V223.2.p: A saint warns someone not to drink from or use a well that has been poisoned.

V223.3.p: A saint knows what another person is thinking and exposes that person's secret sins.

V223.4.p: A saint helps someone learn something, usually by giving them knowledge that would otherwise take effort.

V223.4.1.p: A lazy schoolboy who skips lessons learns a long lesson while sleeping with his head in a saint's lap.

V223.5.p: Saints are given the ability to speak the languages of the people they visit, even when those people are animals or birds.

V223.5.1.p: A saint understands what a wren, a fly, and a cat are saying.

V223.6.p: A saint is able to foretell future events.

V223.6.1.p: A saint is able to predict what the weather will be.

V224.p: Animals or objects belonging to a saint are miraculously replaced after they have been lost, taken, or used up.

V224.1.p: Objects burned as firewood by a saint are miraculously replaced.

V224.2.r: Loomis White Magic 70; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
V224.2.p: Food, or animals used as food, eaten by a saint are miraculously replaced.

V224.3.p: Animals stolen from a saint are miraculously replaced.

V224.4.p: A performing fox that was accidentally killed is miraculously replaced for a saint.

V224.5.p: A supply of lime for building a church is miraculously renewed for a saint.

V225.p: A saint appears in several places at the same time.

V226.r: *Toldo II 99; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
V226.p: Saints live as hermits, withdrawn from ordinary society.

V227.p: Saints are visited by divine beings sent from God.

V227.1.p: God gives a saint the staff of Jesus.

V228.p: Saints and holy men are exempt from certain harms or obligations that ordinary people must bear.

V228.1.p: A saint cannot be harmed by poison. This is one of the immunities that mark holy men as protected by God.

V228.1.1.p: A saint drinks a poison and suffers no injury from it.

V228.2.p: A hermit who lives apart from the world is protected against the spells and power of a magician.

V229.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about saints that do not fit under the more specific headings.

V229.1.p: A saint orders a dead person to return to life and the revived person gives the saint supernatural knowledge.

V229.2.p: A general heading for the many signs and wonders that show a saint's holiness.

V229.2.1.p: A holy infant is repeatedly found lying with its arms stretched out in the shape of a cross.

V229.2.2.p: A holy infant vomits up food that is unclean or forbidden, showing it is sacred.

V229.2.3.p: A saint will drink only the milk of a cow that has been milked by a faithful, pious woman.

V229.2.3.1.p: As a baby, a saint refuses to nurse from his mother's breast on Wednesdays and Fridays, the fast days.

V229.2.4.p: When a child destined to be a wonder-worker is baptized, a range of strange or miraculous events occur.

V229.2.5.p: The spot where a saint was martyred stays green and fresh forever.

V229.2.6.p: When martyrs are wounded, milk flows from their wounds instead of blood.

V229.2.6.1.p: A saint weeps tears of blood.

V229.2.7.p: Flowers grow on the graves of holy people, springing from their mouths or hearts.

V229.2.8.p: A saint's body stays uncorrupted in the ground for a long time after burial.

V229.2.9.p: The tombs of saints give off oil.

V229.2.10.p: Stones respond with "Amen" when a saint preaches to them.

V229.2.11.p: A miracle clears a saint who has been wrongly accused or unjustly criticized.

V229.2.11.1.p: A saint makes a greedy reptile jump from the saint's own body into a bishop's throat and then come back out, proving the bishop wrong to condemn him.

V229.2.12.p: Saints are said to live unusually long lives, a sign of their holiness.

V229.2.12.1.p: Seven Irish saints are said to have never died but remain alive.

V229.2.12.2.p: A saint lives for three hundred (or perhaps one hundred) years without eating food or speaking evil.

V229.2.13.p: A saint promises that he will come back to earth from heaven.

V229.3.p: A saint drives snakes out of a place so that they no longer live there.

V229.4.p: A saint overcomes or destroys monsters, such as dragons.

V229.5.1.p: A saint shuts a monster or dragon up in a lake.

V229.6.p: A saint is in conflict with a druid, a pagan priest or magician.

V229.6.1.p: A saint reduces the power of a druid who satirizes or curses people.

V229.6.2.p: A druid poisons an ale, but a saint miraculously makes it safe again.

V229.6.3.p: A saint lifts a druid into the air, drops him, and his brains are dashed out on a stone.

V229.6.4.p: A druid uses magic spells to try to drive a saint off an island.

V229.7.p: Invading armies are miraculously defeated by saints.

V229.7.1.r: (Cf. D2163.4.) *Loomis White Magic 123; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
V229.7.1.p: A saint drives an army away by sending a thick, smoky cloud over it.

V229.8.p: Saints create a magic mist that hides people or things from view.

V229.9.p: Saints use unusual fuels for their fires, such as burning stone, snow and icicles, a marble pillar, or green timber.

V229.10.p: A saint restores broken objects to their original form.

V229.10.1.p: A saint restores burned clothes to their previous form.

V229.10.2.p: A holy man restores hands and feet that have been cut off.

V229.10.3.p: A saint causes a person's grey hair to grow back black, restoring youthful color.

V229.11.p: A saint has a tongue of literal fire.

V229.12.p: A sinful beauty repents and spends the rest of her life doing penance, as with Mary Magdalene, Mary of Egypt, and Thais.

V229.13.p: The ground rises up to shelter or comfort a saint.

V229.14.p: A saint, angered, shows his great strength by kicking a wall so that it breaks.

V229.15.p: A saint disguised as a poor man saves a king who gave alms from punishment in hell.

V229.16.p: A lake of milk comes into being because of a saint's merit.

V229.17.p: A saint's blessing makes a river the best place for fishing.

V229.18.p: A quarrel between two saints is resolved by an angel.

V229.19.p: Objects mourn the death of a saint or holy man.

V229.20.p: An ascetic or saint falls from his holy state and loses his virtue.

V229.20.1.p: After a holy person has a son, he or she loses their miraculous power.

V229.21.p: A house and family appear overnight to give hospitality to priests caught out after dark.

V229.22.p: The severed head of a saint speaks so that searchers can find it.

V229.23.p: A stone turns red when a picture of a saint is removed from it.

V229.24.p: A saint turns snakes into stones.

V229.25.p: Animals talking together reveal to a man how he can become a saint.

V230.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 26b; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 107, Beal XXI 334; German: Grimm No. 3. For an extensive analysis of angels in Jewish tradition see *Neuman.
V230.p: Angels, supernatural messengers and beings of God.

V230.3.p: A person wrestles or fights with an angel in a struggle between a mortal and a heavenly being.

V231.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
V231.p: An angel shows itself to a person in some visible form.

V231.1.p: An angel appears in the form of a bird.

V231.2.p: A shooting star turns out to be an angel.

V231.3.p: An angel is depicted or appears with four wings.

V231.4.p: An angel takes the appearance of a churchman or priest.

V231.5.p: An angel appears to a woman to warn her not to force a girl into marriage.

V231.6.p: An angel appears as an old man.

V232.r: Spanish: Keller, Espinosa Jr. No. 188; Jewish: *Neuman.
V232.p: An angel acts as a helper to a mortal, aiding them in various ways.

V232.1.r: English: Wells 76 (Joseph of Aramathie); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
V232.1.p: An angel comes to help a person fight in battle.

V232.1.1.p: Angels appear and help a boy prince kill his treacherous uncle.

V232.2.p: An angel carries a mortal from one place to another.

V232.2.0.1.p: An angel carries a boat to the water.

V232.2.0.2.p: An angel carries a saint's staff from place to place.

V232.3.p: Angels bring food to a mortal who needs it.

V232.3.1.p: An angel shows a saint where to dig to find water.

V232.4.p: An angel unfastens a man's chains or shackles.

V232.5.p: An angel leads or guides a mortal along the way.

V232.6.p: An angel reveals where a lost or buried object is hidden.

V232.7.p: Angels bring gifts to holy people or to those they help.

V232.7.1.p: An angel brings a cross to a saint as a gift.

V232.8.p: An angel helps Peter escape from prison.

V232.9.p: An angel cleans a household hearth for someone.

V233.r: *Chauvin VI 184 No. 349; *Fb “engel” I 250; Jewish: *Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas I 313f., 149f., 371ff., 380.
V233.p: The angel of death, who takes people's lives at God's command.

V233.1.r: Type 795*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 795*; Russian: Andrejev No. 795A*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 795*.
V233.1.p: The angel of death spares a mother who is nursing her children; as punishment the angel must serve as a church sexton.

V234.r: *Chauvin VI 106 No. 270; *Loomis White Magic 53; Irish myth: *Cross.
V234.p: Angels sing songs, usually in praise or celebration.

V234.1.p: Angels sing in honor of a saint.

V234.1.1.p: Angels sing to welcome a saint.

V234.1.2.p: Angels sing over the body of a saint.

V234.1.3.p: An angel choir sings in response when a saint receives holy orders.

V234.2.p: Angels sing on the night Christ was born.

V235.r: Irish: Plummer clxxxii, *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 301 No. 16; Spanish: Keller Espinosa Jr. No. 186; Jewish: *Neuman.
V235.p: A mortal person is visited by an angel.

V235.0.1.p: Mortals are visited by an angel in a vision.

V235.0.2.p: An angel is called up or summoned through fasting.

V235.1.p: An angel announces the birth of Christ to shepherds.

V235.2.p: An angel comforts a sinner who repents.

V235.3.p: An angel bars an abbot from his cell because the abbot has expelled a sinning monk.

V236.p: Angels who rebelled against God and were cast out of heaven.

V236.1.p: Angels who fell from heaven turn into fairies, dwarfs, or trolls instead of being cast into hell.

V237.p: An angel stands in the road to block the way of Balaam's donkey.

V238.r: (Cf. F403.2.2.2, V232, 246.) Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
V238.p: A guardian angel is assigned to watch over and protect a person.

V238.1.p: Angels hover over a mortal, usually a saint, as a sign of their protection or holiness.

V238.2.p: Angels melt the snow around a holy infant so that he stays dry and warm.

V238.3.p: Angels singing or serving at a place show that a saint has reached his heavenly destination.

V238.4.p: The air above the grave of a former druid, who was converted to Christianity, is full of angels.

V241.p: Angels pay respect to a mortal by performing honors for him or her.

V241.1.p: Angels attend the funeral of a saint.

V241.1.1.p: An angel tells the people where and how to bury a saint.

V241.2.p: Angels hold a church service over a saint's tomb.

V241.2.1.p: Angels cause light to shine on a saint's tomb.

V241.3.p: Angels hold races in front of a saint as a mark of honor.

V241.4.p: An angel performs the baptism of a saint.

V241.4.1.p: An angel gives a child its name.

V241.5.p: Angels place a heavenly veil on the head of a pious woman as an honor.

V242.p: A holy place or object becomes glorified because an angel is present there.

V242.1.p: A procession of angels rises up out of a graveyard.

V242.2.p: An angel lives or stays in a church.

V242.2.1.p: Angels take part in a church service.

V242.3.p: An angel regularly visits a holy stone or place, and its sacredness is increased by the angel's presence.

V243.p: An angel responds to a human's prayer by granting or answering it.

V243.1.p: Angels appear over the grave of a dead girl because of prayers said for her by her lover, a young monk.

V244.p: An angel keeps pleading at the grave of a sinner who was forgiven, until the body is moved to consecrated ground.

V245.p: An angel punishes a human being.

V245.1.r: (Cf. Q220, Q325, Q458.) Irish myth: Cross.
V245.1.p: An angel whips or scourges a human for disobeying God.

V246.p: An angel gives advice or guidance to a human.

V246.0.1.p: An angel leaves a letter or book containing instructions for a saint.

V246.0.2.p: An angel dictates a book or hands over a book to a human.

V246.1.p: An angel tells a saint the place where he is to build his church.

V246.2.p: An angel serves as a saint's teacher.

V246.3.p: An angel warns a saint that guests are about to arrive.

V247.p: Motifs describing how angels spend their days and lives.

V248.p: Motifs describing the relationship between angels and God.

V249.p: Miscellaneous motifs about angels that do not fit the other groups.

V249.1.p: An angel makes a public announcement or proclamation.

V249.2.p: Angels are said to speak a particular language.

V249.2.1.p: Angels are said to speak Hebrew.

V250.r: **Crane Liber de Miraculis; *DeVooys Middelnederlandse Legenden en Exempelen 57; Genthe Die Jungfrau Maria: ihre Evangelien und ihre Wunder (Halle, 1852); *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 366c. — Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 59, 78, Beal XXI 307, 314, 323, 327; Spanish: Keller, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 202—04. For references in addition to those given below, see volume VI s.v. “Virgin Mary”.
V250.p: Motifs concerning the Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus.

V250.1.p: An Irish saint is called "Mary of the Gael," a title that compares the saint to the Virgin Mary.

V250.2.p: The Virgin Mary is described as having golden hair.

V251.r: (Sometimes resuscitation.) Alphabet No. 464; Ward II 606 No. 14, 633 No. 31, 650 No. 1; *Crane Miraculis Nos. 6, 7, 10, 31, 39; Wells 169 (De Miraculo Beate Marie); Scala Celi 123a, 125b Nos. 674, 681.—Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V251.p: The Virgin Mary holds off a sinner's death so that he has time to repent and receive absolution and save his soul.

V251.1.p: The Virgin Mary restores a man to life after he has seen the torments of hell, so he can repent.

V252.r: Alphabet No. 381; Wesselski Mönchslatein 78 No. 68; *Crane Miraculis No. 34; Icelandic: Boberg.
V252.p: The Virgin Mary comes to the defense of an innocent person who has been accused.

V252.1.r: Ward II 638 No. 10; *Crane Miraculis No. 33; Wells 167 (Vernon Miracles).
V252.1.p: The Virgin Mary repays a borrowed debt that a man entrusted to the sea, and exposes the lender who falsely claims it was never paid.

V252.2.p: The Virgin Mary saves a criminal who is about to be burned at the stake.

V253.p: A person who is devoted to the Virgin Mary is rewarded even if he has not been faithful to Christ.

V254.p: Tales showing how powerful it is to say the Ave (Hail Mary) prayer.

V254.1.r: *Crane Miraculis No. 12; Ward II 605ff. Nos. 10, 18, 20; Herbert III 26; *Crane Vitry 263 No. 296.
V254.1.p: Saying Ave Maria wipes away a person's sins.

V254.1.1.p: A robber hanged on the gallows is held up by the Virgin Mary because he once said Ave Maria.

V254.2.r: (Cf. D2141.1.) *Crane Miraculis No. 28; Ward II 626 No. 9, 640 Nos. 12, 14, 15, *677 No. 12.
V254.2.p: A ship in a storm is saved because the sailors say Ave Maria.

V254.3.p: After a faithful person who always said Ave Maria dies, the words are found printed on his tongue.

V254.3.1.p: A blasphemer is paralyzed in every part of his body except the tongue, which once said Ave Maria.

V254.4.p: A devil is driven out by the words Ave.

V254.5.p: A nun forgets to say the Hail Mary and leaves the convent to live in sin.

V254.6.p: Saint Joseph and the Virgin Mary threaten to leave heaven when a man who always prayed to them is refused entry.

V254.7.r: (Chaucer’s Prioress’s Tale.) **Brown PMLA XXI 486ff.; Ward II 656, 697 and passim; Herbert III 528; Wells Catalogue of Romances 166 (Vernon Miracles).
V254.7.p: A murdered boy keeps singing Ave after he is dead.

V254.7.1.p: A criminal who had said Ave is beheaded, and his head keeps calling out Ave Maria.

V254.8.p: The Virgin Mary will not let the devil or the authorities take a robber-nobleman who says Ave every day.

V254.9.p: The Virgin forbids the devil to take a robber as long as he keeps saying two Aves every day.

V255.r: *Crane Miraculis Nos. 3, 9; Ward II 607 No. 15, 660 No. 29; Scala Celi 116a, 116b Nos. 644, 645; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V255.p: The Virgin Mary arranges for a dissolute monk to be buried in consecrated ground, because the only mass he ever heard was one in her honor.

V255.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
V255.1.p: A devoted follower of the Virgin who is denied burial in consecrated ground is revealed by a lily growing from his mouth, which shows where his grave lies.

V255.2.p: The Virgin secretly celebrates a private mass for a pious woman who cannot attend church.

V256.p: The Virgin Mary performs a miraculous healing.

V256.1.p: Spittle from the Virgin Mary has the power to heal.

V256.2.p: People are healed by miracles performed in front of an image of the Virgin Mary.

V256.3.p: The Virgin Mary restores a hand to Saint John Damascene after he had cut it off to stop himself from lusting.

V256.4.p: At the devil's urging a man castrates himself, and the Virgin Mary saves his life, though she will not restore the severed parts.

V256.5.p: The Virgin Mary brings a drowned man back to life because he had always greeted her with reverence.

V261.p: The Virgin Mary chooses which candidate should win an election to an office.

V261.1.p: The Virgin restores an office to an uneducated man because of his strong faith.

V261.2.p: The Virgin pardons a man who cheated in an election after he repents.

V262.p: The Virgin Mary supplies mead for a hostess of the king who has nothing prepared for a feast.

V263.p: A portrait of the Virgin appears to a devout person.
