V264.r: *Crane Miraculis No. 23; Ward II 612 No. 30; Spanish Exempla: Keller; West Indies: Flowers 580.
V264.p: The Virgin Mary rescues a man who is being attacked by the devil.

V264.1.p: The Virgin Mary brings a man the contract he signed with the devil and frees him from the devil's power.

V265.r: Ward II 634 No. 34, 636 Nos. 7, 41, 667 No. 13, 721 No. 17; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V265.p: The Virgin miraculously stops a nun, or in some versions a monk, from leaving the cloister.

V265.1.r: Crane Vitry 160 No. 60; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V265.1.p: An image of the Virgin tries in vain to keep a nun from leaving the convent.

V266.p: The Virgin Mary converts a Jewish person to Christianity.

V267.p: A devoted follower of the Virgin is comforted at the moment of death.

V268.p: Miracles happen to people who are under the protection of the Virgin Mary.

V268.1.p: A boy who is under the Virgin Mary's protection is pulled alive from a well after a week down there.

V268.2.p: The Virgin Mary rescues a devotee who is about to drown in the waves.

V268.3.p: The Virgin Mary destroys an army of Moors that is besieging Constantinople.

V268.4.p: The Virgin Mary saves the son of a devotee from being wrecked at sea.

V268.5.p: An image or statue of the Virgin Mary performs miracles.

V271.p: The Virgin Mary acts as a foster mother to someone.

V275.r: Ward II 603 No. 6, 606 No. 12, 610 No. 25, 618 No. 39, 648 No. 44; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V275.p: The Virgin Mary offers comfort and forgiveness to criminals who repent.

V276.p: The Virgin Mary appears to a man who has gone astray.

V276.1.p: The Virgin Mary appears to a monk who has strayed and encourages him to pray; in return his prayers weave her a garment.

V276.2.p: The Virgin Mary appears to a monk who was too overworked to pray to her and forgives him.

V276.3.p: The Virgin Mary helps a repentant man who killed a priest; the priest is briefly raised from death to forgive the murderer and then returned to his tomb.

V277.p: The Virgin Mary appears to a devoted follower.

V277.1.r: The nun devoutly prayed to see Him. Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V277.1.p: The Virgin Mary appears to a devout nun while holding the infant Jesus.

V281.p: The Virgin Mary gives a gift to someone devoted to her.

V282.r: Canney Revue de l’Histoire des Religions CXV (1937) 90ff.; Krappe Review of Religion (1948) 376ff.
V282.p: The Virgin Mary is seen as the protector of sailors, known as Stella Maris, the star of the sea.

V283.p: The Virgin Mary makes a testament, a final statement or will.

V284.p: During a flood the Virgin Mary comes down into the streets to rescue her image from the floodwaters.

V290.p: A general heading for sacred persons not covered by the more specific headings.

V291.p: Master poets, called ollamhs, are treated as sacred persons.

V292.p: The twelve apostles of Christ, the close followers of Jesus who are treated as sacred figures in the tale.

V292.1.p: The apostles appear in a story, showing up in person or as visitors in the narrative.

V292.2.p: A group of twelve apostles associated with Ireland, treated as sacred figures in the tale.

V293.p: Lepers are regarded as holy or sacred people, so that they are honored rather than shunned.

V294.p: The pope, the head of the Catholic Church, is treated as a sacred figure in the tale.

V300.p: General heading for tales that deal with religious beliefs and the teachings they embody.

V310.p: General heading for tales that illustrate particular points of church doctrine or dogma.

V311.p: A belief that the soul lives on after death in a future world, and tales that show this belief.

V311.0.1.p: The druids teach that the soul is immortal and lives on after death.

V311.1.p: A man on his deathbed comes to believe in a life after death, though he still feels sure that his new belief will do him no good.

V311.2.p: A dying man refuses to believe that there is any life after death.

V311.3.p: A person offered the choice between staying alive and going to heaven chooses heaven.

V312.r: (Cf. T510.) *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 272a; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V312.p: Belief in the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine that Mary was conceived free of original sin.

V312.1.p: A plague ends when the church proclaims the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.

V312.2.p: A man who opposes the Immaculate Conception dies suddenly after staging a fake miracle to disprove it; he is found to be truly dead, not merely pretending.

V313.p: The Last Judgment, when God judges all people at the end of the world.

V315.p: Belief that Christ's death atoned for human sin, reconciling people with God.

V315.1.p: Repentance has the power to wipe away sin and win forgiveness.

V316.p: Belief that prayer is effective and that God answers those who pray.

V316.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 779*; Russian: Andrejev No. 841I*.
V316.1.p: A hermit, wanting to prove the Gospel saying that whoever asks shall receive, asks for a princess's hand in marriage and then performs the difficult task set for him.

V317.p: The idea that a particular people has been singled out by God as special or chosen above others.

V317.1.p: A holy land is promised to or given to the chosen people as their own.

V320.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 251b; Irish myth: Cross.
V320.p: Stories about people whose religious beliefs are judged to be false or opposed to official doctrine, called heretics.

V321.p: A madman sets fire to a heretic while he lies in bed, and as a reward for this deed his sanity is restored.

V322.p: A heathen is baptized, but the baptism is understood as handing him over to the devil's possession.

V323.p: Stories about people who deny the existence of God, called atheists.

V323.1.p: The ancient Epicureans are regarded as atheists because they did not believe that gods intervene in the world.

V325.p: Water used for baptism disappears when an Arian bishop approaches, showing that his baptism is invalid.

V326.p: A hero refuses to go to heaven because his dead heathen companions are not there.

V327.p: The author of a book written against a heretic is honored by the Virgin Mary and the angels.

V328.p: A man sets fire to his own house and dies in it rather than accept Christianity.

V330.p: A person changes from one religion to another.

V331.r: (Cf. M177.1.) Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 555; Dickson 199 n. 89; Malone PMLA XLIII 413. — Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 65, Beal XXI 325; Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Wells 88 (Roland and Vernagu); Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; Tahiti: Henry Ancient Tahiti (Honolulu, 1928) 178.
V331.p: A person changes to Christianity from another religion.

V331.0.1.p: A Druid, a priest of the ancient Celtic religion, becomes a Christian.

V331.0.2.p: Two or three Irishmen already believe in Christianity before St. Patrick comes to Ireland.

V331.1.r: Dickson 193—98 passim; Alphabet No. 558; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 71, 74, Beal XXI 326; English: Wells 91 (Otuel), 119 (Octovian), *Hibbard 45ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
V331.1.p: A person is converted to Christianity by seeing a miracle.

V331.1.1.p: A person is converted to Christianity after seeing blood flow from an image of Jesus.

V331.1.2.p: A person is converted to Christianity after seeing a cross and angels appear.

V331.1.3.p: A person converts to Christianity after the heathen gods prove weaker than the Christian God.

V331.1.4.p: Neophytes (new converts) are converted after a saint's staff miraculously goes through a convert's foot.

V331.2.p: A person is told to convert to Christianity or be put to death, and accepts Christianity to save their life.

V331.3.r: (Cf. D1860.) English: Wells 122 (The King of Tars).
V331.3.p: A person's appearance is miraculously made beautiful when they convert to Christianity.

V331.4.p: A person converts to Christianity after showing repentance for their sins.

V331.5.p: A person converts to Christianity because of love, often for a Christian lover or spouse.

V331.6.p: A ruler converts to Christianity out of gratitude for kindnesses shown to him in the past. In the note, a captive is baptized and then marries the ruler's sister.

V331.7.p: Saladin, the Muslim sultan, asks to be made a Christian knight.

V331.9.p: Swans, who are enchanted children, no longer suffer in harsh weather once they have converted to Christianity.

V331.10.p: A person converts to Christianity because they admire the virtue of Christians.

V331.10.1.p: A person converts to Christianity after seeing Christians show forgiveness and gentleness.

V332.p: A non-Christian, often called a heathen, is baptized into Christianity.

V340.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
V340.p: A miracle is shown to people who do not believe, to convince them.

V341.r: Result of vision. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 560.
V341.p: A pagan prophetess draws a picture of the Virgin Mary holding the Christ child in the sand, a miracle that shows the truth of Christianity.

V342.p: Jews are frightened and driven off when someone makes the sign of the cross at them.

V343.p: Jews who protest a marriage between a Jewish woman and a Christian man are struck mute.

V344.p: A temple about to be seized by pagans is saved when a sign of the cross or an image of the Virgin appears.

V345.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V345.p: A dove flies out of the mouth of an impious hermit who has agreed to give up his faith for a woman. When he repents, the dove flies back into his mouth.

V346.p: A doubter who mocks the faith is kicked by a sacrificial animal, showing the power of the sacrifice.

V347.p: Idols are found lying face down on the ground after a saint arrives, showing their powerlessness.

V350.p: Different religions come into conflict with one another.

V351.r: Dickson 187 nn. 61, 62; English: Wells 88 (Roland and Vernagu), 91 (Otuel); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V351.p: A formal debate or contest is held to decide which religion is superior.

V351.1.p: A wise non-believer or heretic is defeated in a debate with a Christian.

V351.1.1.p: A Brahmin wins a discussion about religion against an opponent.

V351.2.p: A non-believer loses an argument to a hermit.

V351.3.p: A magician is overpowered in a contest against a holy man or saint.

V351.3.1.p: St. Peter competes against Simon Magus, a magician, and prevails.

V351.4.p: Two religions settle which is better by holding a contest of prayer.

V351.5.p: A yogi and a Muslim compete by displaying miraculous powers to show which religion is better.

V352.r: English: Wells 76 (Joseph of Aramathie); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V352.p: A pagan who argues with a Christian is struck dumb.

V352.1.p: A pagan debating a Christian is defeated when God puts the right words into the Christian's mouth.

V354.p: The life of a heroic age is said to be better than living as a Christian.

V355.p: Buddhists become slaves of Taoists because they cannot make rain.

V356.p: A Christian hero or saint destroys heathen idols.

V356.1.p: A saint drives pagan devils out of ancient shrines.

V356.2.p: Pagan shrines, idols, or magic books are destroyed by fire sent from heaven.

V356.2.1.p: Through a saint's power, heathen idols sink into the earth up to their necks.

V356.3.p: When a saint points his crozier (bachall) at an idol, the idol is defaced.

V360.p: Christian and Jewish traditions and stories about each other.

V361.r: (Hugh of Lincoln.) (Cf. V254.7.) **V. Manzini La superstizione omicida e i sacrifici umani, con particolare riguardo alle accuse contro gli Ebrei (2d ed., Padua, 1930); **Berger Mélusine VIII 169ff.; *Ward II 656 No. 3; *Brown PMLA XXI 486ff. — English: Child III 240ff., IV 497a.
V361.p: A Christian child is killed so that his blood can be used in a Jewish ritual.

V362.r: German: H. Rauchfuss Alte Geschichte u. neue Sagen aus Thuringen 60.
V362.p: Jews are blamed for causing a plague by poisoning the wells. This is an antisemitic accusation found in Christian tradition.

V363.r: Preserved by Virgin Mary. *Ward II 601; Irish myth: Cross (V35.1.0.1); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V363.p: A Jewish father throws his child into an oven as punishment for the child taking communion (the eucharist) in a Christian church. This is an antisemitic legend.

V363.1.p: After the Jewish child is burned to ashes for eating consecrated bread in a Christian church, the child is brought back to life through the power of the Virgin Mary.

V364.r: C55, J1261.2, V30). He kills the other priest who saw him commit the sacrilege, and before killing, forces him to renounce his faith. A miracle exposes the murderer. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3270, Legends Nos. 416ff.
V364.p: A Jew who has converted to Christianity becomes a priest. During Mass he stabs the consecrated host, and blood flows from it.

V365.p: Customs and practices of Jews as they relate to non-Jews, as seen in Christian tradition.

V380.p: A general heading for religious beliefs that do not fit the more specific categories in this section.

V381.r: (Cf. V123.) *Boje 101; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 238 No. 185.
V381.p: A non-Christian believer (a heathen) strikes or beats his god after suffering bad luck.

V382.p: A doctor mocks the belief in the Devil, Heaven, and Hell.

V383.p: Excessive or extreme religious zeal, where devotion becomes dangerous or absurd.

V383.1.p: A person dies because they kneel or lie prostrate in worship for too long.

V383.2.p: A Hindu accidentally drinks water from a Muslim's vessel, and as a result his luck turns bad.

V385.p: The Romans refuse to include Jesus among their gods because of his poverty, which they despise.

V400.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 111c; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V400.p: A general heading for the religious virtue of giving to those in need.

V410.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 22, Beal XXI 307, 337; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 137, 200—204; Jewish: *Neuman.
V410.p: Acts of charity are rewarded, often by God or by some supernatural means.

V410.1.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 131; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 87 No. 756E*.
V410.1.p: Giving to charity is rewarded more highly than praying or attending masses.

V410.2.p: A prince takes as his motto the saying that charity conquers all.

V411.p: Charitable giving is rewarded by a miracle.

V411.1.p: A queen gives away a sleeve of her dress, and the sleeve is miraculously restored.

V411.2.p: A saint exchanges his coat with a beggar, and gold sleeves miraculously appear on the coat.

V411.3.p: A man who has given away everything in charity has a foot cut off, and the foot is miraculously restored.

V411.4.p: A money-lender who generously lends to the poor finds that stones turn to gold for him as a reward for his charity. The note adds that because of this, lenders never refuse money borrowed for a wedding.

V411.5.p: A saint gives away treasure, and God miraculously restores it to the giver.

V411.5.1.p: A man in his present life receives back as much wealth as he gave to charity in a previous life.

V411.6.p: A saint gives away food, and God miraculously restores the food that was given away.

V411.7.p: A generous king gives something to a beggar, then blows his nose and finds a huge ruby in his handkerchief as a miraculous reward.

V411.8.p: When a man gives his cloak to a beggar, Jesus appears to him as a reward. The motif is named for St. Martin.

V411.9.p: A person who does a charitable act is miraculously rewarded when a flame settles on their forehead.

V412.p: Miraculous events happen while a person is in the act of giving charity.

V412.1.p: St. Nicholas steals bread in order to feed the poor, and the bread is miraculously restored.

V412.2.p: The more flour or bread the monks give to the poor, the more God fills their storage bins.

V413.p: A son's charitable deeds save his dead father's soul from punishment.

V414.p: A saint shares the punishment of a sinful man because the saint once shared his own cloak with that man during life.

V415.p: Children are jealous of the money their dead father gave to a bishop. In a vision they find a receipt showing that he was repaid more than a hundredfold.

V416.p: An act of charity wipes out a person's sin.

V416.1.p: A man convicted of cheating in his bookkeeping is forgiven when it is discovered that he gave the stolen money to the poor.

V420.p: Stories about the punishments that befall people who refuse to be charitable.

V421.p: A sailor refuses to give alms, and his ship is turned to stone as punishment.

V422.p: A stingy knight bargains even while giving alms, and he is devoured by serpents. The note says his gift of corn turns into serpents.

V425.p: A pope who was uncharitable in life wanders as a restless ghost after death.

V430.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs about charity that do not fit the more specific categories.

V431.r: Alphabet Nos. 260, 754, 786, 789, 792; Irish: Beal XXI 337; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 213.
V431.p: A usurer gives charity, but it does no good because the money was gotten by unjust lending.

V432.p: A man gives away so much in charity that he impoverishes himself.

V433.p: Saints show charity to others, often by giving generously to the poor or needy.

V434.p: A conqueror returns a kingdom to a king because of an act of charity the king once performed.

V435.p: A pious man gives charity to someone who had earlier refused to give him charity.

V436.p: A mendicant friar or beggar refuses alms offered by a barren woman.

V437.p: A saint repeatedly gives away his father's property to the poor, against the father's wishes.

V438.p: A person loses the spiritual reward for a charitable deed when he asks for work or payment in return.

V440.p: Other tales about religious virtues that do not fit the more specific categories.

V441.p: A person pardons someone who has wronged him.

V441.1.p: A saint heals an enemy who has harmed him or his people, returning kindness for hatred.

V450.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 384a, 389b; Irish myth: Cross.
V450.p: Tales about religious orders, which are groups of people living under a rule in a monastery or convent.

V451.p: A family dedicates its firstborn son, and one out of every ten children born afterward, to the Church.

V453.p: The Levites, a priestly tribe, are presented as a religious order.

V460.p: Tales about the good and bad qualities of clergy, such as monks, nuns and priests.

V461.p: Good qualities expected of clergy, such as obedience, honesty, chastity and submission.

V461.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 690; Alphabet No. 322; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V461.1.p: A nun who is obedient and hardworking is considered the most worthy member of the convent.

V461.2.p: A truthful monk refuses to cheat or lie, even when cheating would benefit his religious order.

V461.3.p: Chastity, or sexual purity, is presented as a clerical virtue.

V461.4.p: Submission, or humble obedience to authority, is presented as a clerical virtue.

V461.4.1.p: A clergyman is praised for always telling the truth, counted as a virtue in a religious person. It falls under submission as a clerical virtue.

V461.5.p: A religious person is praised for spending long periods in deep prayerful thought, which is counted as a clerical virtue.

V461.6.p: A monk lives among people who speak badly of him, so that he is not tempted by flattery and stays out of danger.

V461.7.p: A man captured by robbers trusts so completely that God will protect him that he is saved. The virtue is absolute faith in a cleric.

V461.8.p: A religious person is praised for choosing poverty, which is counted as a saintly virtue.

V462.r: *Loomis White Magic 111f.; *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 42b; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
V462.p: Asceticism: a religious person practices severe self-denial, such as fasting, silence, or hardship, as a spiritual discipline.

V462.0.1.p: A king gives up his throne to live as an ascetic in religious self-denial.

V462.0.2.p: Someone argues that because salvation is already predestined, ascetic practices are pointless.

V462.0.3.p: A husband leaves his wife to become an ascetic and live a religious life of self-denial.

V462.0.4.p: A murderer turns to asceticism as a religious penance for his crime.

V462.1.r: Alphabet Nos. 709, 711, 712, 725; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 310 No. 32; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V462.1.p: A religious person practices keeping silence as a form of self-discipline.

V462.2.r: Alphabet Nos. 24, 145; Wesselski Mönchslatein 170 No. 135; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
V462.2.p: A religious person practices fasting as a form of self-denial.

V462.2.1.r: Alphabet Nos. 22, 23; Scala Celi 4a No. 16; India: Thompson-Balys.
V462.2.1.p: An ascetic who is fasting makes his suffering worse by setting food and drink in front of himself and not eating it.

V462.2.2.p: A person turns down rich delicacies, choosing plain fare instead.

V462.2.2.1.p: A saint refuses a gift of pearls and asks for ordinary food instead.

V462.2.3.p: Someone dies as a result of severe fasting and other ascetic devotions.

V462.3.p: A religious person weeps constantly as an act of ascetic devotion.

V462.4.p: A religious person denies himself all rest as a form of asceticism.

V462.4.1.p: A cleric practices continual kneeling and bowing as an ascetic discipline.

V462.4.2.p: A cleric keeps an all-night vigil standing with his hands stretched out in the shape of a cross.

V462.4.3.p: A saint keeps one hand raised toward heaven even while doing everyday tasks such as eating or reaping. This shows extreme self-denial, never allowing himself rest.

V462.5.p: An ascetic, a devout religious man who denies himself comforts, punishes or inflicts pain on his own body.

V462.5.0.1.p: An ascetic cleric prays that he may become diseased, seeking suffering as a form of holiness.

V462.5.1.p: An ascetic cleric wears a garment made of rough hair as a form of penance that makes his body suffer.

V462.5.1.1.p: A saint refuses woolen clothing and wears only the skins of wolves and other wild animals.

V462.5.1.2.p: An ascetic cleric sleeps, or prays, with a wet sheet or cloak wrapped around him, enduring the cold as penance.

V462.5.2.p: An ascetic cleric sleeps on a bed of stone instead of a soft bed, as a form of self-punishment.

V462.5.2.1.p: A saint sleeps only a very little, denying himself rest.

V462.5.2.2.p: A saint stays standing for seven years without sleeping at all.

V462.6.p: An ascetic cleric refuses to listen to music, avoiding even this pleasure as a denial of the senses.

V462.7.p: An ascetic cleric never smiles or laughs, showing his strict withdrawal from worldly pleasure.

V462.8.p: An ascetic submerges himself in water as a form of religious discipline.

V462.8.1.p: A saint shuts himself inside a narrow pen during Lent as a period of strict penance.

V462.8.2.p: A saint stands, apparently asleep, while a bird builds a nest and hatches her young in his hand, showing his stillness and holiness.

V462.9.p: An ascetic cleric lives as a beggar, depending on alms and charity from others.

V462.10.p: An ascetic cleric lives for seven years on the back of a whale, withdrawn from ordinary life.

V462.11.p: An ascetic cleric gives up the world and becomes a herder of animals.

V462.12.p: A monk turns down a chance to have his temptation removed, because he thinks it makes him stronger to face it constantly as a test.

V462.13.p: A wicked religious hermit misuses magic powers he gained through prayer and meditation.

V462.14.p: A boy spends twelve years trying to wash off the dirt of an ascetic, who has never bathed or cleaned himself.

V463.p: A religious person is killed for his faith, dying as a martyr.

V463.1.p: A cleric gives up his own life so that his body can consecrate (bless and make holy) the ground he is buried in.

V463.2.p: John the Baptist is named as the first Christian martyr, the first to die for the faith.

V464.p: Someone punishes or tortures their own body in order to become holy or win God's favor.

V465.p: A general heading for sins and faults of members of the clergy, such as lust, greed, and dishonesty.

V465.1.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 113b, 136c; West Indies: Flowers 580.
V465.1.p: Clergy who break their vow of chastity and have sexual relations.

V465.1.1.p: A monk or priest who is unchaste and sins with women.

V465.1.1.1.p: A monk seduces a girl, then murders her, and afterwards turns away from the faith to become an unbeliever.

V465.1.1.2.p: Clergy marry, going against the rule that priests and monks must not marry.

V465.1.2.p: A nun who breaks her vow of chastity and has sexual relations.

V465.1.2.1.p: An abbess hides a nun from a pursuing knight, but the nun then reveals her own hiding place to him. He later abandons her.

V465.1.2.2.p: A man tempts a nun into sin by telling her that God cannot see what happens in the dark.

V466.p: Simony: the buying or selling of church offices or holy things for money.

V466.1.p: A pope is guilty of simony, having bought or sold church office for money.

V467.p: A priest reads a cookbook instead of the breviary (the daily prayer book the clergy are required to recite).

V468.p: A priest is paid off or bribed to reveal what was confessed to him in confession.

V470.p: A general heading for stories about people taking vows to join a religious order or become clergy.

V471.p: Someone is cured of a disease after taking clerical vows.

V472.p: A person takes clerical vows and joins the church after being disappointed in love.

V472.1.p: A man becomes a hermit after realizing that his beloved's love for him was selfish.

V473.p: A former monk refuses payment for his work because he regards the work as a religious duty.

V475.p: A religious person gives up the vows they took when entering a religious order or the clergy, and returns to ordinary secular life.

V475.1.p: A monk who has left his order is punished, and dies in torment for having abandoned his vows.

V475.2.p: A monk who has left his order is forgiven, and a miracle returns him to his religious life.

V475.3.p: A man who has become disappointed with his religious order gives up his vow and leaves it.

V475.4.p: A saint leaves his religious order because he loves music too much.

V475.5.p: A hermit who lives alone in religious seclusion is tempted by money to go back to ordinary worldly life.

V510.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 632b; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
V510.p: Miscellaneous religious visions, in which a holy person sees or experiences something divine or supernatural.

V510.1.p: God appears to a devout person and speaks to them in a vision.

V510.2.p: Only a man who is completely without sin is able to see God.

V511.p: A person sees a vision of the other world, meaning heaven, hell, or a similar realm beyond death.

V511.1.r: **Becker Medieval Visions of Heaven and Hell (Baltimore, 1899); **Ward II 396ff. passim; Alphabet No. 622, 743; Dickson 265; Scala Celi 66a, 138b Nos. 362, 777. — Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 57, Beal XXI 322; English: Malory Morte D’Arthur XV 3; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 105 No. 932; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
V511.1.p: A person sees a vision of heaven.

V511.1.1.p: Saints are granted visions of heaven.

V511.1.2.p: A person sees angels guarding the road to heaven against devils.

V511.2.r: *Becker (see V511.1); Alphabet No. 610; Dickson 265; Herbert III 25; **Ward II 386ff.; *Crane Vitry 260f. No. 289; Scala Celi 34b, 74a, 85b Nos. 195, 422, 497. — Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
V511.2.p: A person sees a vision of hell.

V511.2.1.p: A person sees a vision of the fires of hell.

V511.2.2.p: A person sees a vision of the gate of hell.

V511.2.3.p: A girl has a vision of her mother being punished in hell. She chooses to live the poor life her father lived, which leads to heaven.

V511.3.p: A person sees a vision of purgatory, the place where souls are purified before entering heaven.

V511.4.p: A person sees a vision of the Land of the Saints, a blessed realm of holy people.

V512.p: A man sees a vision of his own soul being judged after death.

V512.1.r: He is saved. Ward II 651 No. 5; *Herbert III 471.
V512.1.p: A clerk sees his good and evil deeds being weighed in a vision of judgment, and asks that his faith in Christ (or the Virgin) be placed on the scale.

V512.2.p: A man whose only good deed was done by accident sees that single deed outweigh all his sins when his deeds are weighed in judgment.

V513.p: Saints receive miraculous visions from God.

V513.1.p: A saint is instructed or guided by a vision.

V513.2.p: A saint sees in a vision the earth caught in the devil's snares.

V514.p: Visions that have no religious meaning, such as ordinary or secular dream-visions.

V515.p: Visions in which the things seen stand for something else, each image representing a hidden meaning.

V515.1.p: Allegorical visions with a religious meaning.

V515.1.1.p: In a vision, the seats or thrones prepared in heaven are seen, made of gold, silver, or crystal, and each saint's seat is given according to his merit.

V515.1.2.p: A wife sees the moon enter her husband's mouth and the husband sees a star enter his wife's mouth, a sign that a famous child, a saint, will be born.

V515.1.3.p: A saint sees a vision of flames covering Ireland that are quenched except for sparks, and then a great light appears and dispels the darkness; the flames stand for the faith brought by Saint Patrick, which fades until it is restored by a later saint.

V515.1.3.1.p: In a vision, when a shower falls, a small stone grows larger and a large stone wastes away; this shows the present and future state of the Irish church.

V515.1.3.2.p: A swineherd sees in a vision a yew tree on a rock, with an oratory in front of it and angels climbing up and down from it; a druid interprets this as the founding of Cashel and the royal line of Munster.

V515.1.4.p: Constantine sees a vision of the Cross.

V515.1.5.p: A person sees a vision of dry bones, which stands for a symbolic message about restoration or revival.

V515.2.p: Allegorical visions with a political meaning, in which the images stand for people, families, or events in a kingdom.

V515.2.1.p: A chieftain sees in a vision a pair of gray seals sucking at his two breasts; they stand for two of his allies who are being overpowered by invaders.

V515.2.1.1.p: A king sees in a vision a whelp he raised gather dogs of Ireland and Britain against him, but in the end the whelp is killed in battle; the whelp stands for one of the king's two foster sons.

V515.2.2.p: A saint foresees in a vision, through allegory, the future of a king's family, and the Cross is part of the meaning.

V515.2.3.p: A king sees in a vision his four sons changed into a lion, a greyhound, a beagle, and a cur, which fight with alternating success until the lion defeats the other three.

V516.p: A religious person is shown a vision of what will happen in the future.

V520.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics Index 517b; Irish myth: Cross.
V520.p: A person is saved, meaning rescued from sin or spiritual ruin and granted salvation.

V522.p: A sinner changes his ways after being shown heaven and hell in a visit.

V523.p: A king is saved, but only in spite of his own wishes or behavior, the only such king of his kind.

V525.p: A sinner who thinks of God at the end is saved, while a religious devotee whose mind is on worldly things goes to hell.

V526.p: Worshiping a particular god is rewarded with rebirth in the world of Brahma.

V530.p: Journeys undertaken to sacred places for religious reasons.

V531.p: A journey made to the Holy Land for religious devotion.

V531.1.p: A pilgrim follows the roads that Christ is said to have walked during the Holy Land journey.

V532.p: A journey made to Mecca for religious devotion.

V533.p: A journey made to Benares, a holy city, for religious devotion.

V535.p: A journey made to Jerusalem for religious devotion.

V540.p: A person is saved from death or harm by divine providence, meaning God's guiding care.

V541.p: A man is kept from boarding a ship that later sinks, so he survives.

V542.p: A man hears a voice warning him to leave a dangerous spot in a mine, and he is saved.
